claim: The prd-2 gene mutation is characterized by recessive inheritance of a long 26 hr period phenotype.
source: Here, we show that the prd-2 (period-2) gene, whose mutation is characterized by recessive inheritance of a long 26 hr period phenotype, encodes an RNA-binding protein that stabilizes the ck-1a transcript, resulting in CKI protein levels sufficient for normal rhythmicity.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing the period length of prd-2 mutants throughout the manuscript.

claim: PRD-2 encodes an RNA-binding protein that stabilizes the ck-1a transcript.
source: Here, we show that the prd-2 (period-2) gene, whose mutation is characterized by recessive inheritance of a long 26 hr period phenotype, encodes an RNA-binding protein that stabilizes the ck-1a transcript, resulting in CKI protein levels sufficient for normal rhythmicity.
evidence: Supported by RNA stability assays showing reduced ck-1a half-life in Δprd-2 mutants and CLIP experiments demonstrating direct binding of PRD-2 to ck-1a transcript.

claim: PRD-2 stabilization of ck-1a results in CKI protein levels sufficient for normal rhythmicity.
source: Here, we show that the prd-2 (period-2) gene, whose mutation is characterized by recessive inheritance of a long 26 hr period phenotype, encodes an RNA-binding protein that stabilizes the ck-1a transcript, resulting in CKI protein levels sufficient for normal rhythmicity.
evidence: Supported by data showing reduced CKI protein levels in Δprd-2 mutants and rescue of the long period phenotype by hyperactive CKI or increased ck-1a expression.

claim: The Nonsense-Mediated Decay pathway has a strong influence on CKI levels.
source: Moreover, by examining the molecular basis for the short circadian period of upf-1prd-6 mutants, we uncovered a strong influence of the Nonsense-Mediated Decay pathway on CKI levels.
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data showing elevated ck-1a levels in Δupf1prd-6 mutants and protein data showing increased CKI levels in NMD mutants.

claim: Circadian period defects in prd-2 and upf1prd-6 mutants each arise from disruption of ck-1a regulation.
source: The finding that circadian period defects in two classically derived Neurospora clock mutants each arise from disruption of ck-1a regulation is consistent with circadian period being exquisitely sensitive to levels of casein kinase I.
evidence: Supported by genetic epistasis experiments, RNA and protein level measurements, and rescue experiments manipulating CKI levels.

claim: Circadian period is exquisitely sensitive to levels of casein kinase I.
source: The finding that circadian period defects in two classically derived Neurospora clock mutants each arise from disruption of ck-1a regulation is consistent with circadian period being exquisitely sensitive to levels of casein kinase I.
evidence: Supported by data showing that both increases and decreases in CKI levels affect period length, and by prior literature cited in the manuscript.

claim: The Neurospora circadian oscillator is a transcription–translation feedback loop positively regulated by the White Collar Complex (WCC) transcription factors.
source: The Neurospora circadian oscillator is a transcription–translation feedback loop that is positively regulated by the White Collar Complex (WCC) transcription factors, which drive expression of the negative arm component Frequency (FRQ).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: The fungal core circadian oscillator shares a common regulatory architecture with the mammalian core clock.
source: In this way the fungal core circadian oscillator shares a common regulatory architecture with the mammalian core clock.
evidence: This is established knowledge based on comparative studies of circadian clocks across species.

claim: The circadian negative arm complex in Neurospora is composed of FRQ, FRH, and CKI.
source: In Neurospora, the circadian negative arm complex is composed of FRQ and FRQ-interacting RNA helicase (FRH), which together bring casein kinase I (CKI) to promote phosphorylation of WCC on key phospho-sites to inhibit its activity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by prior literature cited in the text.

claim: FRQ, FRH, and CKI promote phosphorylation of WCC on key phospho-sites to inhibit its activity.
source: In Neurospora, the circadian negative arm complex is composed of FRQ and FRQ-interacting RNA helicase (FRH), which together bring casein kinase I (CKI) to promote phosphorylation of WCC on key phospho-sites to inhibit its activity (Wang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference Wang et al., 2019.

claim: FRQ is extensively regulated transcriptionally, translationally, and post-translationally over the circadian day leading ultimately to its inactivation.
source: FRQ is extensively regulated transcriptionally, translationally, and post-translationally over the circadian day leading ultimately to its inactivation (reviewed in: Hurley et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the cited review.

claim: Negative arm components FRQ and PER are regulated by anti-sense transcription.
source: Negative arm components FRQ and PER are regulated by anti-sense transcription (Koike et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2003), by thermally regulated splicing (Colot et al., 2005; Majercak et al., 1999), and display characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Negative arm components FRQ and PER are regulated by thermally regulated splicing.
source: Negative arm components FRQ and PER are regulated by anti-sense transcription (Koike et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2003), by thermally regulated splicing (Colot et al., 2005; Majercak et al., 1999), and display characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: FRQ and PER display characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins.
source: Negative arm components FRQ and PER are regulated by anti-sense transcription (Koike et al., 2012; Kramer et al., 2003), by thermally regulated splicing (Colot et al., 2005; Majercak et al., 1999), and display characteristics of intrinsically disordered proteins (Pelham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: FRQ, PERs, and CRYs undergo progressive phosphorylation leading to their inactivation.
source: Another highly conserved feature of fungal, insect, and mammalian negative arm components is progressive phosphorylation leading to their inactivation (Baker et al., 2009; Ode et al., 2017; Vanselow et al., 2006) (reviewed in: Dunlap and Loros, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CKI orthologs are highly conserved in sequence and function across eukaryotic clocks.
source: In contrast, less is known about the mechanisms regulating expression of the other essential member of the negative arm complex, CKI, orthologs of which are highly conserved in sequence and in function across eukaryotic clocks.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: CKI forms a stable complex as FRQ–FRH–CKIa in Neurospora.
source: CKI forms a stable complex as FRQ–FRH–CKIa in Neurospora (Baker et al., 2009; Görl et al., 2001), as PER-DOUBLETIME (DBT) in flies (Kloss et al., 2001), and as a multi-protein complex of PER-CRY-CKIδ in mouse (Aryal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CKI forms a complex as PER-DOUBLETIME (DBT) in flies.
source: CKI forms a stable complex as FRQ–FRH–CKIa in Neurospora (Baker et al., 2009; Görl et al., 2001), as PER-DOUBLETIME (DBT) in flies (Kloss et al., 2001), and as a multi-protein complex of PER-CRY-CKIδ in mouse (Aryal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CKI forms a multi-protein complex of PER-CRY-CKIδ in mouse.
source: CKI forms a stable complex as FRQ–FRH–CKIa in Neurospora (Baker et al., 2009; Görl et al., 2001), as PER-DOUBLETIME (DBT) in flies (Kloss et al., 2001), and as a multi-protein complex of PER-CRY-CKIδ in mouse (Aryal et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Fungal CKI phosphorylates both FRQ and WCC.
source: Fungal CKI phosphorylates both FRQ and WCC (He et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Insect DBT and mammalian CKIδ/ε are key regulators of the PER2 phospho-switch.
source: Insect DBT and mammalian CKIδ/ε are key regulators of the PER2 phospho-switch, differentially phosphorylating two regions that control PER2 turnover (Top et al., 2018; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CKI phosphorylations contribute to feedback loop closure in all species.
source: Thus, CKI phosphorylations contribute to feedback loop closure in all species.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion of CKI function across species.

claim: FRQ–CKI binding strength is a key regulator of period length.
source: FRQ–CKI binding strength is a key regulator of period length and an important oscillator variable first described in Neurospora (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CKI abundance is not rhythmic in any species described to date.
source: CKI abundance is not rhythmic in any species described to date (Görl et al., 2001; Kloss et al., 2001), but preliminary evidence suggests that its expression levels are tightly controlled to keep the clock on time, just like FRQ/PER/CRY.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CKI expression levels are tightly controlled to keep the clock on time.
source: CKI abundance is not rhythmic in any species described to date (Görl et al., 2001; Kloss et al., 2001), but preliminary evidence suggests that its expression levels are tightly controlled to keep the clock on time, just like FRQ/PER/CRY.
evidence: This is supported by inference from the data presented in the manuscript and cited literature.

claim: In mammals, CKI knockdown or knockout significantly lengthens period.
source: In mammals, CKI knockdown or knockout significantly lengthens period (Isojima et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Tsuchiya et al., 2016), and CKIδ levels are negatively regulated by m6A methylation (Fustin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: CKIδ levels are negatively regulated by m6A methylation.
source: In mammals, CKI knockdown or knockout significantly lengthens period (Isojima et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Tsuchiya et al., 2016), and CKIδ levels are negatively regulated by m6A methylation (Fustin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In Neurospora, decreasing the amounts of the casein kinase I (ck-1a) transcript using a regulatable promoter leads to long period defects up to ~30 hr.
source: In Neurospora, decreasing the amounts of the casein kinase I (ck-1a) transcript using a regulatable promoter leads to long period defects up to ~30 hr (Mehra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by data in Figure 4A.

claim: CKI has a conserved C-terminal domain involved in autophosphorylation and inhibition of kinase activity.
source: CKI has a conserved C-terminal domain involved in autophosphorylation and inhibition of kinase activity (Gietzen and Virshup, 1999; Guo et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Fungal mutants lacking the CKI C-terminal inhibitory domain have hyperactive kinase activity.
source: Fungal mutants lacking this CKI C-terminal inhibitory domain have hyperactive kinase activity (Querfurth et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by data in Figure 4B.

claim: The circadian period is sensitive to CKI abundance and activity due to its importance in circadian feedback loop closure.
source: Across clock models, the circadian period is sensitive to CKI abundance and activity due to its importance in circadian feedback loop closure.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion and supported by data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Forward genetic screens used the ras-1bd mutant background in race tube assays to identify key players in the circadian clock.
source: Forward genetic screens used the ras-1bd mutant background (which forms distinct bands of conidiophores once per subjective night) in race tube (RT) assays to identify key players in the circadian clock (Belden et al., 2007; Feldman and Hoyle, 1973; Sargent et al., 1966).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: prd-4 encodes checkpoint kinase 2 (Chk2) and links the clock to cell-cycle progression.
source: prd-4 (period-4), encoding checkpoint kinase 2 (Chk2), links the clock to cell-cycle progression (Pregueiro et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: prd-3 encodes casein kinase II (CKII) and implicates direct phosphorylation of core clock proteins as central to temperature compensation.
source: prd-3 (period-3), encoding casein kinase II (CKII), implicated direct phosphorylation of core clock proteins as central to temperature compensation (Mehra et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: prd-1 encodes an essential RNA-helicase that regulates the core clock under high nutrient environments.
source: prd-1 (period-1) encodes an essential RNA-helicase that regulates the core clock under high nutrient environments (Emerson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: prd-6 encodes the core UPF1 subunit of the Nonsense-Mediated Decay (NMD) complex.
source: prd-6 (period-6, hereafter referred to as upf1prd-6) encodes the core UPF1 subunit of the Nonsense-Mediated Decay (NMD) complex (Compton, 2003), although its circadian role remains cryptic.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The upf1prd-6 short period phenotype is completely epistatic to the prd-2 mutant's long period.
source: Equipped with the identity of PRD-2, we then followed up on the observation that the upf1prd-6 short period phenotype is completely epistatic to the prd-2 mutant's long period (Morgan and Feldman, 1997; Morgan and Feldman, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references and confirmed by data in Figure 5A.

claim: UPF1PRD-6 and PRD-2 use distinct mechanisms to play opposing roles in regulating levels of the casein kinase I transcript.
source: We find that UPF1PRD-6 and PRD-2 use distinct mechanisms to play opposing roles in regulating levels of the casein kinase I transcript in Neurospora, thus rationalizing the circadian actions of the two clock mutants whose roles in the clock were not understood.
evidence: This is supported by data showing PRD-2 stabilizes ck-1a while NMD degrades it.

claim: The endogenous ck-1a transcript has a strikingly long 3'-UTR.
source: The endogenous ck-1a transcript has a strikingly long 3'-UTR, indicating that its mRNA could be subject to NMD during a normal circadian day.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5C showing ck-1a has one of the longest 3'-UTRs in the genome.

claim: The long 3'-UTR of ck-1a indicates that its mRNA could be subject to NMD during a normal circadian day.
source: The endogenous ck-1a transcript has a strikingly long 3'-UTR, indicating that its mRNA could be subject to NMD during a normal circadian day.
evidence: This is inferred from the known mechanism of NMD targeting long 3'-UTR transcripts.

claim: upf1prd-6 mutants have elevated levels of ck-1a in the absence of NMD.
source: We confirm that upf1prd-6 mutants have elevated levels of ck-1a in the absence of NMD, and further rescue the short period defect of upf1prd-6 mutants by titrating down ck-1a mRNA levels using an inducible promoter.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data in Figure 5B and protein data in Figure 5F.

claim: The short period defect of upf1prd-6 mutants can be rescued by titrating down ck-1a mRNA levels using an inducible promoter.
source: We confirm that upf1prd-6 mutants have elevated levels of ck-1a in the absence of NMD, and further rescue the short period defect of upf1prd-6 mutants by titrating down ck-1a mRNA levels using an inducible promoter.
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5D showing period rescue at low QA concentrations.

claim: The casein kinase I transcript is subject to complex regulation by NMD and PRD-2 to control its gene expression and maintain a normal circadian period.
source: Taken together, a unifying model emerges to explain the action of diverse period mutants, where the casein kinase I transcript is subject to complex regulation by NMD and an RNA-binding protein, PRD-2, to control its gene expression and maintain a normal circadian period.
evidence: This is the main conclusion inferred from all the experimental data presented.

claim: Whole genome sequencing revealed a 322 kb inversion on chromosome V in the prd-2INV mutant.
source: PCR data consistent with this prompted whole genome sequencing that revealed a 322 kb inversion on chromosome V (Lambreghts, 2012) in the original isolate strain hereafter referred to as prd-2INV.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and confirmed by sequencing data in Figure 1A and B.

claim: The left breakpoint of the inversion occurs in the 5'-UTR of NCU03775.
source: The left breakpoint of the inversion occurs in the 5'-UTR of NCU03775, and its upstream regulatory sequences are displaced in the prd-2INV mutant.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A knockout of NCU03775 has a wild-type circadian period length.
source: However, a knockout of NCU03775 (FGSC12475) has a wild-type circadian period length, unlike the long period prd-2INV mutant (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The right breakpoint of the inversion occurs in the 5'-UTR of NCU01019, disrupting 333 bases of its 5'-UTR and its entire promoter region.
source: The right breakpoint of the inversion occurs in the 5'-UTR of NCU01019, disrupting 333 bases of its 5'-UTR and its entire promoter region (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: A knockout of NCU01019 has a 26 hr long period, matching the prd-2INV long period phenotype.
source: A knockout of NCU01019 has a 26 hr long period, matching the prd-2INV long period phenotype (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The prd-2INV mutant has drastically reduced levels of NCU01019 gene expression in constant light conditions and in the subjective evening of a circadian free run.
source: The prd-2INV mutant has drastically reduced levels of NCU01019 gene expression in constant light conditions and in the subjective evening of a circadian free run (Figure 1D), suggesting that the inversion completely disrupts the NCU01019 promoter and TSS.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1D by RT-qPCR data.

claim: The long period length of prd-2 occurs at very low gene expression levels of NCU01019 using 10−6 M quinic acid induction.
source: Placing NCU01019 under the nutrient-responsive qa-2 promoter, we find that the long period length occurs at very low gene expression levels using 10−6 M quinic acid induction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Ectopic expression of NCU01019 at the csr-1 locus in the prd-2INV background rescues the long period phenotype.
source: Finally, ectopic expression of NCU01019 at the csr-1 locus in the prd-2INV background rescues the long period phenotype (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1F.

claim: PRD-2 is encoded by NCU01019.
source: We conclude that PRD-2 is encoded by NCU01019.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and molecular data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Both the SUZ domain and the proline-rich C-terminus of PRD-2 are required for a normal clock period.
source: We mapped the clock-relevant domains of the PRD-2 protein (Figure 2A), finding that both an SUZ domain and the proline-rich C-terminus of PRD-2 are required for a normal clock period.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and C by domain deletion experiments.

claim: The SUZ domain family can bind RNA directly in vitro.
source: The SUZ domain family can bind RNA directly in vitro (Song et al., 2008), but curiously PRD-2's adjacent R3H domain, which is better characterized in the literature as a conserved RNA-binding domain, is dispensable for clock function.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: PRD-2's R3H domain is dispensable for clock function.
source: The SUZ domain family can bind RNA directly in vitro (Song et al., 2008), but curiously PRD-2's adjacent R3H domain, which is better characterized in the literature as a conserved RNA-binding domain, is dispensable for clock function.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2B and C where R3H deletion mutants have wild-type period.

claim: The C-terminus of PRD-2 is predicted to be highly disordered.
source: The C-terminus of PRD-2 is predicted to be highly disordered, and finer mapping of this region showed that neither a glutamine/proline-rich domain (amino acids 525–612, 21% Gln, 26% Pro) nor a domain conserved across fungal orthologs (amino acids 625–682, 21% Pro) were required for normal clock function (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is inferred from the high proline content and supported by domain analysis.

claim: PRD-2 SUZ domain and C-terminal deletion mutants are expressed at the protein level.
source: Further, PRD-2 SUZ domain and C-terminal deletion mutants are expressed at the protein level, indicating that clock defects must be due to the absent domain (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A by western blot.

claim: PRD-2 is exclusively localized to the cytoplasm based on biochemical evaluation.
source: PRD-2 is exclusively localized to the cytoplasm based on biochemical evaluation, and this localization does not change as a function of time of day (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D by subcellular fractionation.

claim: PRD-2 localization does not change as a function of time of day.
source: PRD-2 is exclusively localized to the cytoplasm based on biochemical evaluation, and this localization does not change as a function of time of day (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2D by time course fractionation.

claim: NCU01019 RNA expression is not induced by light.
source: NCU01019 RNA expression is not induced by light (Wu et al., 2014) nor rhythmically expressed over circadian time (Hurley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: NCU01019 RNA is not rhythmically expressed over circadian time.
source: NCU01019 RNA expression is not induced by light (Wu et al., 2014) nor rhythmically expressed over circadian time (Hurley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: NCU01019 protein is abundant and shows weak rhythms.
source: NCU01019 protein is abundant and shows weak rhythms (Hurley et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which suggests that PRD-2 oscillations are driven post-transcriptionally to peak in the early subjective morning, prior to the peak in the frq transcript (Aronson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: PRD-2 oscillations are driven post-transcriptionally to peak in the early subjective morning, prior to the peak in the frq transcript.
source: NCU01019 protein is abundant and shows weak rhythms (Hurley et al., 2018; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), which suggests that PRD-2 oscillations are driven post-transcriptionally to peak in the early subjective morning, prior to the peak in the frq transcript (Aronson et al., 1994).
evidence: This is inferred from the protein rhythms data and cited reference on frq transcript timing.

claim: Rhythms in PRD-2 protein expression were confirmed using a luciferase translational fusion, which peaked during the circadian day.
source: Rhythms in PRD-2 protein expression were confirmed using a luciferase translational fusion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C), which peaked during the circadian day.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: prd-2INV and ΔNCU01019 have a slight growth defect.
source: prd-2INV and ΔNCU01019 have a slight growth defect (Figure 1C) and are less fertile than wild type as the female partner in a sexual cross (data not shown).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1C and mentioned as unpublished observation.

claim: prd-2INV and ΔNCU01019 are less fertile than wild type as the female partner in a sexual cross.
source: prd-2INV and ΔNCU01019 have a slight growth defect (Figure 1C) and are less fertile than wild type as the female partner in a sexual cross (data not shown).
evidence: This is mentioned as an unpublished observation.

claim: Temperature and nutritional compensation of ΔNCU01019 alone are normal.
source: Temperature and nutritional compensation of ΔNCU01019 alone are normal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), which was expected given the normal TC profile of the prd-2INV mutant (Gardner and Feldman, 1981).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and supported by the cited reference.

claim: PRD-2 is well conserved among Ascomycota fungi as noted by BLASTp scores (<e-70).
source: PRD-2 (XP_961631.1) is well conserved among Ascomycota fungi as noted by BLASTp scores (<e-70), while only its R3H and/or SUZ domains have significant similarity to insect and mammalian proteins: the encore gene in flies and the R3HDM1, R3HDM2, and ARPP21 genes in human and mouse.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Only PRD-2's R3H and/or SUZ domains have significant similarity to insect and mammalian proteins.
source: PRD-2 (XP_961631.1) is well conserved among Ascomycota fungi as noted by BLASTp scores (<e-70), while only its R3H and/or SUZ domains have significant similarity to insect and mammalian proteins: the encore gene in flies and the R3HDM1, R3HDM2, and ARPP21 genes in human and mouse.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic analysis.

claim: Hundreds of genes are affected by loss of PRD-2.
source: To identify the putative mRNA targets of PRD-2, we performed total RNA-sequencing on triplicate samples of Δprd-2 versus control grown in constant light at 25°C. Hundreds of genes are affected by loss of PRD-2, but we did not identify a consensus functional category or sequence motif(s) for the putative PRD-2 regulon (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 from RNA-seq data.

claim: No consensus functional category or sequence motif was identified for the putative PRD-2 regulon.
source: To identify the putative mRNA targets of PRD-2, we performed total RNA-sequencing on triplicate samples of Δprd-2 versus control grown in constant light at 25°C. Hundreds of genes are affected by loss of PRD-2, but we did not identify a consensus functional category or sequence motif(s) for the putative PRD-2 regulon (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: PRD-2 plays multiple roles in the cell, including regulation of carbohydrate and secondary metabolism.
source: Given the pleotropic phenotypes of Δprd-2, we posit that PRD-2 plays multiple roles in the cell, including regulation of carbohydrate and secondary metabolism.
evidence: This is inferred from the RNA-seq data and functional enrichment analysis.

claim: ck-1a, frq, wc-2, ckb-1, and frh were significantly altered in the absence of PRD-2.
source: Focusing specifically on core clock genes, we found that ck-1a, frq, wc-2, ckb-1 (regulatory beta subunit of CKII), and frh were significantly altered in the absence of PRD-2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3A from RNA-seq data.

claim: The CKI transcript was dramatically less stable in Δprd-2.
source: Pursuing the top two hits, we found that the CKI transcript was dramatically less stable in Δprd-2 (Figure 3B), while frq mRNA stability was not significantly altered (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3B by RNA stability assay.

claim: frq mRNA stability was not significantly altered in Δprd-2.
source: Pursuing the top two hits, we found that the CKI transcript was dramatically less stable in Δprd-2 (Figure 3B), while frq mRNA stability was not significantly altered (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: PRD-2 binds the ck-1a transcript in vivo.
source: ck-1a is also enriched in the PRD-2 CLIP sample, demonstrating that the CKI transcript is a direct target of the PRD-2 protein (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 3C by CLIP experiment.

claim: Increasing expression of ck-1a using high levels of QA partially rescued the Δprd-2 long period phenotype.
source: We found that increasing expression of ck-1a using high levels (10−1 to 10−2 M) of QA partially rescued the Δprd-2 long period phenotype (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a synergistic poor growth defect in the Pqa-2-ck-1a Δprd-2 double mutant at 10−4 M QA, consistent with low levels of ck-1a.
source: We also noticed a synergistic poor growth defect in the double mutant at 10−4 M QA, consistent with low levels of ck-1a (an essential gene in Neurospora: Görl et al., 2001; He et al., 2006).
evidence: This is observed in Figure 4A and supported by cited references showing ck-1a is essential.

claim: ck-1a is an essential gene in Neurospora.
source: We also noticed a synergistic poor growth defect in the double mutant at 10−4 M QA, consistent with low levels of ck-1a (an essential gene in Neurospora: Görl et al., 2001; He et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: The CKISHORT mutation is completely epistatic to Δprd-2.
source: Significantly, the CKISHORT mutation is completely epistatic to Δprd-2 (Figure 4B), indicating that CKI is the clock-relevant target of PRD-2.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CKI is the clock-relevant target of PRD-2.
source: Significantly, the CKISHORT mutation is completely epistatic to Δprd-2 (Figure 4B), indicating that CKI is the clock-relevant target of PRD-2.
evidence: This is concluded from the epistasis experiment in Figure 4B.

claim: Open reading frames in 5'-UTRs that produce short peptides (5'-uORFs) can trigger NMD in Neurospora crassa.
source: Open reading frames in 5'-UTRs that produce short peptides (5'-uORFs) can trigger NMD in a mechanism that does not require the Exon Junction Complex (EJC; Zhang and Sachs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The frq transcript has six 5'-uORFs.
source: The frq transcript has six such uORFs (Colot et al., 2005; Diernfellner et al., 2005) and could be a bona fide NMD target because its splicing is disrupted in the absence of NMD (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: frq could be a bona fide NMD target because its splicing is disrupted in the absence of NMD.
source: The frq transcript has six such uORFs (Colot et al., 2005; Diernfellner et al., 2005) and could be a bona fide NMD target because its splicing is disrupted in the absence of NMD (Wu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Transcripts containing long 3'-UTRs are subject to NMD regulation.
source: Transcripts containing long 3'-UTRs are also subject to NMD regulation.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the NMD field.

claim: Transcripts with intron(s) near a STOP codon and/or with intron(s) in the 3'-UTR can be degraded by NMD after recruitment of the UPF1/2/3 complex by the EJC.
source: In addition, transcripts with intron(s) near a STOP codon and/or with intron(s) in the 3'-UTR can be degraded by NMD after recruitment of the UPF1/2/3 complex by the EJC in a pioneering round of translation (Zhang and Sachs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Loss of NMD reduces the amount of the transcript encoding the short-FRQ protein isoform.
source: Because loss of NMD reduces the amount of the transcript encoding the short-FRQ protein isoform (Wu et al., 2017), and strains making only short-FRQ have slightly lengthened periods (Liu et al., 1997), Wu et al., 2017 recently speculated that the short period of the upf1prd-6 mutant might be explained by effects of NMD on FRQ.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Strains making only short-FRQ have slightly lengthened periods.
source: Because loss of NMD reduces the amount of the transcript encoding the short-FRQ protein isoform (Wu et al., 2017), and strains making only short-FRQ have slightly lengthened periods (Liu et al., 1997), Wu et al., 2017 recently speculated that the short period of the upf1prd-6 mutant might be explained by effects of NMD on FRQ.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Strains expressing only long-FRQ display an essentially wild-type period length.
source: However, strains expressing only long-FRQ display an essentially wild-type period length (Colot et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1997), not a short period phenotype like upf1prd-6; this finding is not consistent with FRQ being the only or even principal clock-relevant target of NMD, leaving unresolved the role of NMD in the clock.
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: FRQ is not the only or even principal clock-relevant target of NMD.
source: However, strains expressing only long-FRQ display an essentially wild-type period length (Colot et al., 2005; Liu et al., 1997), not a short period phenotype like upf1prd-6; this finding is not consistent with FRQ being the only or even principal clock-relevant target of NMD, leaving unresolved the role of NMD in the clock.
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of long-FRQ only strains with upf1prd-6 mutants.

claim: upf1prd-6 is completely epistatic to prd-2INV.
source: To tackle this puzzle, we returned to classical genetic epistasis experiments and confirmed the observation that upf1prd-6 is completely epistatic to prd-2INV (Morgan and Feldman, 2001), going on to show that in fact each of the individual NMD subunit knockouts, ∆upf2 and ∆upf3 as well as Δupf1prd-6, is epistatic to the Δprd-2 long period phenotype (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A and supported by the cited reference.

claim: Each of the individual NMD subunit knockouts (∆upf1, ∆upf2, and ∆upf3) is epistatic to the Δprd-2 long period phenotype.
source: To tackle this puzzle, we returned to classical genetic epistasis experiments and confirmed the observation that upf1prd-6 is completely epistatic to prd-2INV (Morgan and Feldman, 2001), going on to show that in fact each of the individual NMD subunit knockouts, ∆upf2 and ∆upf3 as well as Δupf1prd-6, is epistatic to the Δprd-2 long period phenotype (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A.

claim: ck-1a was the most affected core clock gene in Δupf1prd-6.
source: Previous work had profiled the transcriptome of Δupf1prd-6 compared to a control (Wu et al., 2017); we re-processed this RNA-seq data and found, exactly as in Δprd-2, that ck-1a was the most affected core clock gene in Δupf1prd-6 (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5B from re-analysis of published RNA-seq data.

claim: The ck-1a transcript has an intron located 70 nt away from its longest isoform's STOP codon.
source: The ck-1a transcript has an intron located 70 nt away from its longest isoform's STOP codon, and its 3'-UTR is, remarkably, among the 100 longest annotated UTRs in the entire Neurospora transcriptome (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C from genome annotation analysis.

claim: The ck-1a 3'-UTR is among the 100 longest annotated UTRs in the entire Neurospora transcriptome.
source: The ck-1a transcript has an intron located 70 nt away from its longest isoform's STOP codon, and its 3'-UTR is, remarkably, among the 100 longest annotated UTRs in the entire Neurospora transcriptome (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5C.

claim: NMD targeting to long 3'-UTR transcripts like ck-1a is thought to occur independently of the EJC and nuclear cap-binding complex (CBC) in Neurospora crassa.
source: NMD targeting to long 3'-UTR transcripts like ck-1a is thought to occur independently of the EJC and nuclear cap-binding complex (CBC) in Neurospora crassa (Zhang and Sachs, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Neurospora CBC is not required for a normal circadian clock.
source: We used the knockout mutant Δcbp80 (NCU04187) to confirm that Neurospora CBC is not required for a normal circadian clock and that the long period length of Δprd-2 is unchanged in the Δcbp80 background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The long period length of Δprd-2 is unchanged in the Δcbp80 background.
source: We used the knockout mutant Δcbp80 (NCU04187) to confirm that Neurospora CBC is not required for a normal circadian clock and that the long period length of Δprd-2 is unchanged in the Δcbp80 background (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: ck-1a is a strong candidate for NMD-mediated degradation via its long 3'-UTR, not dependent on EJC and CBC components.
source: Thus, ck-1a is a strong candidate for NMD-mediated degradation via its long 3'-UTR, not dependent on EJC and CBC components.
evidence: This is inferred from the long 3'-UTR data and the CBC independence experiment.

claim: CKI is overexpressed in the absence of NMD, leading to faster feedback loop closure and a short circadian period.
source: We hypothesized that CKI is overexpressed in the absence of NMD (Figure 5B), leading to faster feedback loop closure and a short circadian period.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by subsequent experimental data in Figure 5D-F.

claim: At low levels of inducer (10−5 M QA), decreased levels of ck-1a transcript revert the short period length of Δupf1prd-6 to control period lengths.
source: To genetically control ck-1a levels, we crossed the regulatable Pqa-2-ck-1a allele into the Δupf1prd-6 background and confirmed our hypothesis by finding that at low levels of inducer (10−5 M QA), decreased levels of ck-1a transcript revert the short period length of Δupf1prd-6 to control period lengths (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Protein levels of CKI in the Δupf1prd-6 background are reduced to control levels at 10−5 M QA.
source: Further, protein levels of CKI in the Δupf1prd-6 background are reduced to control levels at 10−5 M QA (Figure 5E), which explains the period rescue phenotype.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CKI protein is two to three times more abundant in Δupf1prd-6 and in Δprd-2 Δupf1prd-6.
source: CKI protein is two to three times more abundant in Δupf1prd-6 and in Δprd-2 Δupf1prd-6 (Figure 5F), matching its overexpression in the Δupf1prd-6 transcriptome (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CKI protein is 3× reduced in Δprd-2.
source: CKI protein is 3× reduced in Δprd-2 (Figure 5F), also correlating with its reduced mRNA expression and stability (Figure 3).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F.

claim: CKI is the clock-relevant target of UPF1PRD-6.
source: We conclude that CKI is also the clock-relevant target of UPF1PRD-6, placing NMD, PRD-2, and CKI in the same genetic epistasis pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic and molecular data presented.

claim: NMD, PRD-2, and CKI are in the same genetic epistasis pathway.
source: We conclude that CKI is also the clock-relevant target of UPF1PRD-6, placing NMD, PRD-2, and CKI in the same genetic epistasis pathway.
evidence: This is concluded from the epistasis experiments and molecular data.

claim: The mechanistic basis of action of two independently derived non-targeted clock mutants (prd-2 and upf1prd-6) centers on regulation of the activity of CKI via two distinct mechanisms.
source: By uncovering the identity and mode of action of PRD-2 and exploring the mechanism of two classical period mutants, prd-2 and upf1prd-6, we found a common basis in regulation of CKI levels, which are under tight control in the Neurospora clock (Figure 6). That the mechanistic basis of action of two independently derived non-targeted clock mutants centers on regulation of the activity of a single enzyme, CKI, via two distinct mechanisms is noteworthy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion from all the data presented.

claim: The predominantly cytoplasmic localization of PRD-2 is consistent with its action in protecting ck-1a transcripts from NMD.
source: The predominantly cytoplasmic localization of PRD-2 (Figure 2D) is consistent with its action in protecting ck-1a transcripts from NMD and rounds out the model.
evidence: This is inferred from the localization data and the proposed mechanism.

claim: PTBP1 protects its target transcripts from NMD-mediated degradation by binding in the 3'-UTR and blocking NMD recruitment in mouse.
source: PTBP1, an RNA-binding protein, protects its target transcripts from NMD-mediated degradation by binding in the 3'-UTR and blocking NMD recruitment in mouse (Ge et al., 2016), and future work will determine if PRD-2 functions similar to PTBP1.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Future work will determine if PRD-2 functions similar to PTBP1.
source: PTBP1, an RNA-binding protein, protects its target transcripts from NMD-mediated degradation by binding in the 3'-UTR and blocking NMD recruitment in mouse (Ge et al., 2016), and future work will determine if PRD-2 functions similar to PTBP1.
evidence: This is speculation about future research directions.

claim: The mammalian PER2 anti-sense transcript displays nearly identical dynamics to qrf expression.
source: The mammalian PER2 anti-sense transcript displays nearly identical dynamics to qrf expression (Koike et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Mammalian PER2 sense expression levels are regulated by microRNA binding sites in its 3'-UTR.
source: Mammalian PER2 sense expression levels are further regulated by microRNA binding sites in its 3'-UTR (Yoo et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: frq RNA is directly targeted for turnover by rhythmic exosome activity in the late day.
source: In a similar manner, frq RNA is directly targeted for turnover by rhythmic exosome activity in the late day (Guo et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: The codons composing the frq transcript are non-optimal, which improves FRQ's co-translational folding.
source: The codons composing the frq transcript are non-optimal, which improves FRQ's co-translational folding (Zhou et al., 2013), and FRQ's disordered protein structure is also stabilized by its binding partner FRH (Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: FRQ's disordered protein structure is stabilized by its binding partner FRH.
source: The codons composing the frq transcript are non-optimal, which improves FRQ's co-translational folding (Zhou et al., 2013), and FRQ's disordered protein structure is also stabilized by its binding partner FRH (Hurley et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Mammalian PER2 is largely intrinsically disordered.
source: Mammalian PER2 is also largely intrinsically disordered, and indeed circadian clock proteins across species have large stretches of intrinsic disorder which are in the early stages of functional characterization (Pelham et al., 2020; Pelham et al., 2018) (reviewed in: Partch, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Circadian clock proteins across species have large stretches of intrinsic disorder.
source: Mammalian PER2 is also largely intrinsically disordered, and indeed circadian clock proteins across species have large stretches of intrinsic disorder which are in the early stages of functional characterization (Pelham et al., 2020; Pelham et al., 2018) (reviewed in: Partch, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: UPF1PRD-6 and the NMD machinery target ck-1a mRNA for degradation to regulate its expression levels, presumably mediated by the long 3'-UTR of ck-1a transcripts.
source: UPF1PRD-6 and the NMD machinery target ck-1a mRNA for degradation to regulate its expression levels, presumably mediated by the long 3'-UTR of ck-1a transcripts in Neurospora (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by data in Figure 5 showing elevated ck-1a in NMD mutants.

claim: NMD components are not rhythmic in abundance in the fungal clock.
source: NMD components are not rhythmic in abundance in the fungal clock (Hurley et al., 2014; Hurley et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: NMD regulation of CKI occurs throughout the circadian cycle.
source: These data, taken together with the constitutive expression of the CKI mRNA and protein (Baker et al., 2009; Görl et al., 2001; Hurley et al., 2014; Hurley et al., 2018), lead us to predict that NMD regulation of CKI occurs throughout the circadian cycle.
evidence: This is predicted based on the non-rhythmic nature of NMD components and CKI.

claim: The discovery of NMD regulation of CKI represents a wholly novel and potentially important mode of regulation for this pivotal kinase.
source: To our knowledge the discovery of NMD regulation of CKI represents a wholly novel and potentially important mode of regulation for this pivotal kinase.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the finding.

claim: Long UTR length appears to be conserved across CKI orthologs.
source: Future work will investigate whether insect DBT and/or mammalian CKIδ/ε (CSNK1D, CSNK1E) are also targets of NMD. Long UTR length appears to be conserved across CKI orthologs (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: A circadian period defect was reported in tissue-specific NMD knockdown in Drosophila, but the behavioral rhythm was lengthened unlike the short period defect in Neurospora.
source: One previous study in Drosophila reported a circadian period defect in a tissue-specific NMD knockdown (Ri et al., 2019), but the behavioral rhythm was lengthened in UPF1-depleted insects unlike the short period defect observed in Neurospora.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: In mouse, both CKIε and CLOCK display altered splicing patterns in the absence of UPF2.
source: In mouse, both CKIε and CLOCK display altered splicing patterns in the absence of UPF2 (Weischenfeldt et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Most core clock proteins have at least one uORF in mammals.
source: Most core clock proteins have at least one uORF in mammals (Millius and Ueda, 2017), altogether raising the possibility that multiple core clock genes are regulated by NMD.
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Multiple core clock genes may be regulated by NMD.
source: Most core clock proteins have at least one uORF in mammals (Millius and Ueda, 2017), altogether raising the possibility that multiple core clock genes are regulated by NMD.
evidence: This is speculation based on the cited reference and findings in this study.

claim: Alternative splicing leads to NMD turnover for four core clock and accessory mRNAs in plants: GRP7, GRP8, TOC1, and ELF3.
source: The importance of NMD has already been recognized and investigated in the plant clock, where alternative splicing leads to NMD turnover for four core clock and accessory mRNAs: GRP7, GRP8, TOC1, and ELF3 (reviewed in: Mateos et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited review.

claim: Low levels of CKI driven from an inducible promoter lead to long periods approaching 30 hr.
source: Low levels of CKI driven from an inducible promoter lead to long periods approaching 30 hr (Mehra et al., 2009; Figure 4A).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference and data in Figure 4A.

claim: In the mammalian clock, decreased CKI expression significantly lengthens period.
source: In the mammalian clock, decreased CKI expression also significantly lengthens period (Isojima et al., 2009; Lee et al., 2009; Tsuchiya et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: A CKI mutant expressing only the shortest CKI isoform has a 17.5 hr short period phenotype in the absence of C-terminal autophosphorylation.
source: We generated a CKI mutant expressing only this shortest CKI isoform, finding a 17.5 hr short period phenotype in the absence of C-terminal autophosphorylation (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Increased CKI activity and/or abundance would be expected to increase FRQ-CKI affinity and lead to faster feedback loop closure.
source: Based on prior work, increased CKI activity and/or abundance would be expected to increase FRQ-CKI affinity and lead to faster feedback loop closure (Liu et al., 2019), consistent with the short period phenotype.
evidence: This is inferred from the cited reference and the observed short period phenotype.

claim: The CKI short isoform is expressed at levels similar to the full length isoform in Neurospora.
source: Curiously, this CKI short isoform is expressed at levels similar to the full length isoform in Neurospora (as well as a third short isoform derived from an alternative splice acceptor event) (Figure 5F), and all isoforms interact with FRQ by immunoprecipitation (Querfurth et al., 2007).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5F and supported by the cited reference.

claim: All CKI isoforms interact with FRQ by immunoprecipitation.
source: Curiously, this CKI short isoform is expressed at levels similar to the full length isoform in Neurospora (as well as a third short isoform derived from an alternative splice acceptor event) (Figure 5F), and all isoforms interact with FRQ by immunoprecipitation (Querfurth et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Mammalian alternative isoforms CKIδ1 and CKIδ2 have different substrate preferences in vitro.
source: Mammalian alternative isoforms CKIδ1 and CKIδ2 have different substrate preferences in vitro, which leads to differential phosphorylation of PER2 whereby CKIδ2 phosphorylation significantly stabilizes PER2 (Fustin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CKIδ2 phosphorylation significantly stabilizes PER2.
source: Mammalian alternative isoforms CKIδ1 and CKIδ2 have different substrate preferences in vitro, which leads to differential phosphorylation of PER2 whereby CKIδ2 phosphorylation significantly stabilizes PER2 (Fustin et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CKIδ1 and CKIδ2 isoform expression patterns appear to be tissue specific and are regulated by m6A RNA modification.
source: Adding further complexity, CKIδ1 and CKIδ2 isoform expression patterns appear to be tissue specific and are regulated by m6A RNA modification.
evidence: This is inferred from the preceding discussion and cited literature.

claim: Regulation of CKI levels and isoform expression is an important direction for future work in the circadian clock.
source: Regulation of CKI levels and isoform expression is an important direction for future work in the circadian clock.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: CKI has a diverse array of functions in eukaryotes and is critically important in human health.
source: CKI has a diverse array of functions in eukaryotes and is critically important in human health (reviewed in: Cheong and Virshup, 2011; Vielhaber and Virshup, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reviews.

claim: CKI overexpression is pathogenic in Alzheimer's disease.
source: CKI overexpression is pathogenic in Alzheimer's disease in addition to its role in circadian period regulation (Sundaram et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Mutation of hPER2 at residue S662 is associated with the human sleep and circadian disorder FASPS.
source: Mutation of hPER2 at residue S662 is associated with the human sleep and circadian disorder FASPS (Toh et al., 2001), and CKIδ/CKIε kinases control the phosphorylation state of this critical site as well as phospho-switch regions dictating PER2 stability (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018; Philpott et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: CKIδ/CKIε kinases control the phosphorylation state of hPER2 S662 as well as phospho-switch regions dictating PER2 stability.
source: Mutation of hPER2 at residue S662 is associated with the human sleep and circadian disorder FASPS (Toh et al., 2001), and CKIδ/CKIε kinases control the phosphorylation state of this critical site as well as phospho-switch regions dictating PER2 stability (Narasimamurthy et al., 2018; Philpott et al., 2020; Zhou et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by the cited references.

claim: Mutation of human CKIδ leads to FASPS.
source: Significantly, mutation of human CKIδ itself phenocopies this, also leading to FASPS (Xu et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the cited reference.

claim: Future work on the regulation of CKI levels and isoform expression will shed light on CKI regulation in the clock, in development, and in human disease.
source: Future work on the regulation of CKI levels and isoform expression will shed light on CKI regulation in the clock, in development, and in human disease.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.
